comparison: Sec 5.2 (RQ2) Table 4, input-component ablation: VulMaster full vs '-w/o AST' ("excluding the AST traversals")
model_config: Same in both arms: adapted-CodeT5 in the FiD framework, fine-tuned (Adam, batch 64, 20 epochs, max 10 segments x 512 tokens); the ablated variant is a model trained without AST segments (retraining procedure not separately described)
dataset_metric: CVEFixes + Big-Vul merged C/C++ repair dataset (VulRepair split, deduplicated); Exact Match (Top-1)
budget_control: Partial cap only: FiD max 10 segments of 512 tokens in both arms, but the AST arm adds AST node-sequence segments and the authors note ~90% of samples use fewer than 10 segments, so the cap rarely binds; the AST arm is longer. Not controlled
arm_a: Full input: whole vulnerable function (segmented) + serialized AST node sequence (DFS traversal, segmented) + CWE knowledge (name, CWE examples, ChatGPT-generated fixes)
arm_b: Same input without the AST node-sequence segments
other_changes: none (same FiD architecture, relevance-prediction task and model adaptation; only the AST input segments are dropped, at training and inference)
delta: Table 4: EM 20.0 (full) vs 19.0 (-w/o AST), i.e. -1.0 pp; text: "the complete function, structural information, and CWE knowledge bring 6%, 5%, and 5.5% improvements" (relative)
rationale: Removing the AST only removes input segments from the same model ("(2) VulMaster w/o AST: excluding the AST traversals"), but the AST is added as extra segments on top of the full function, and the 10x512 segment cap is not binding for ~90% of samples, so the structured arm carries more context. Representation is confounded with input amount.

comparison: Sec 5.4 (RQ4) Table 10: C1 SPVR (full prompt) vs C2 Without_MET_info
model_config: Same in both arms: ChatGPT-3.5-turbo-0125, "same settings as RQ2"
dataset_metric: CVEFixes C/C++ subset, 547 samples; Pass@3 (exact match to ground truth in any of 3 outputs) and CodeBLEU
budget_control: Not controlled; the MET arm adds MET-derived repair instructions to a prompt that is otherwise identical, so it is longer
arm_a: CWE-related information + MET-related (AST minimum-edit-tree derived) repair instructions + regenerated code
arm_b: CWE-related information + regenerated code (MET-related information removed)
other_changes: none reported as a pipeline component; note SPVR generates "up to three MET-related prompts" per sample, each combined with the CWE prompt and regenerated code, so the number/diversity of prompts behind Pass@3 may also differ between arms (not described for the ablation arm)
delta: Table 10: Pass@3 138 vs 55 (of 547); CodeBLEU 0.4456 vs 0.2646; text: "The pass@3 rate decreases to 55/547, representing a loss of over 50% compared to the baseline"
rationale: Same model and dataset, and C2 only "remove[s] the MET-related information from the prompt", but the structured arm is the baseline plus extra AST-derived instructions with no budget control, so structure is confounded with added guidance text (which is also directive repair advice, not just a representation).

comparison: Sec IV-D1 (RQ3) Table III: LLM4FPM (eCPG-Slicer + FARF) vs LLM4FPM-noslice
model_config: Same in both arms: qwen2.5-32b, locally deployed; ablations use "the same experimental configurations as those for LLM4FPM on this dataset"
dataset_metric: Juliet (SAST warnings from Cppcheck/Infer/CSA, 7 CWEs; 7,194 warnings per arm); Accuracy and F1
budget_control: Structured arm shorter: the slice is a subset of the FARF-identified files; the unsliced arm feeds complete files and overflows the context window on 40 cases
arm_a: eCPG line-level slice over the FARF-identified dependent files + bug report
arm_b: Complete content of the same FARF-identified files + bug report ("Instead of slicing the code, the complete content of the files identified by the FARF algorithm is directly fed to the LLM")
other_changes: none (same FARF file selection, prompt and model); the 40 context-overflow cases in the noslice arm are counted as errors in Table III
delta: Table III: Accuracy 98.17% vs 95.15% (+3.02 pp), F1 98.92% vs 97.19% (+1.73 pp); "LLM4FPM-noslice additionally fails on 40 test cases because the input files exceeded the LLM's context window limit"
rationale: Same model, dataset and configuration; the only change is whether the FARF files are sliced or passed whole, and the sliced (structured) arm is the shorter one. Part of the gap comes from the 40 overflow failures of the longer arm, which favours the structured arm by budget rather than against it. (The -nofarf arm, by contrast, changes file retrieval and is a component ablation.)

comparison: Sec 5.6 (RQ6) Tables 7-8: MoCQ (DSL subset) vs DSL100 (complete DSL spec); DSL0 (no spec) appears only in Table 7
model_config: Same in all arms: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, temperature 0.2, Joern backend, same feedback loop and "same iteration threshold" (20 iterations)
dataset_metric: Table 7: 212 generation examples, query-generation pass rate; Table 8: test set, per-vulnerability-type F1 (average over 12 types)
budget_control: Structured-context arm shorter: the subset cuts Joern's DSL by 48% of APIs (CodeQL 67%), so MoCQ's prompt carries less spec than DSL100; iteration budget fixed. (DSL0 vs MoCQ: MoCQ arm longer, not controlled)
arm_a: Curated DSL subset (API signatures, types, functionality) in the query-generation prompt
arm_b: DSL100: complete DSL specification (DSL0: no specification)
other_changes: none between arms (symbolic validator, feedback, generalization and FP-elimination present in all); the varied context is the query-language specification, not the program representation, which is the same Joern CPG in every arm
delta: Table 7 pass rate 77.4% (MoCQ) vs 50.0% (DSL100) vs 9.9% (DSL0); Table 8 average F1 0.51 vs 0.31 (DSL100). Text gives DSL100 pass rate as 49.1%, inconsistent with Table 7's 50.0%
rationale: "We compare MoCQ with DSL subsetting against two variants: (1) DSL100 with a complete DSL specification (no subsetting) and (2) DSL0 with no specification" under the same model, loop and iteration threshold, and the subset arm is shorter, so MoCQ vs DSL100 meets R-strict. Caveat for the survey: this isolates grammar-spec context, not a code representation, so it should not be counted as evidence that program structure helps; DSL0 vs MoCQ alone would be R-unmatched-budget.

comparison: Sec 5.2 (RQ2) Table 2: full vs w/o RAG, w/o AST, w/o PoV (record's headline is w/o RAG, -29 pp)
model_config: Same in all arms: GPT-4o (temperature 0) for Reflector, Grader and Expert agents; OpenAI text-embedding-3-small; Qdrant, similarity threshold 0.35
dataset_metric: 57 Java applications (Transfer benchmark + GitHub); precision, recall, F1, accuracy at application level
budget_control: Not reported per arm; the agentic retrieval loop runs "until the Reflector judges that the current fragment set provides sufficient inter-procedural context", so context amount varies by arm
arm_a: Full: AST-guided segmentation -> embedding index -> multi-agent (Reflector/Grader) iterative cross-file retrieval -> Expert agent with PoV test
arm_b: w/o RAG: "only the target function that invokes the vulnerable API is provided as context" (w/o AST: line-based chunking feeding the same agentic RAG; w/o PoV: PoV test omitted)
other_changes: w/o RAG removes the multi-agent Reflector/Grader retrieval loop (a pipeline stage and tool loop); w/o AST changes the retrieval index units, which changes what the agentic loop retrieves and how many iterations it runs
delta: Table 2 F1: 89% full vs 60% w/o RAG (-29 pp), 64% w/o AST (-25 pp), 77% w/o PoV (-12 pp)
rationale: The cited headline arm removes the agentic retrieval stage, not just a representation ("w/o RAG, where only the target function ... is provided as context"). The closest representation arm, w/o AST ("AST-guided code segmentation is replaced with naive line-based chunking"), still acts through the retrieval loop with unreported context amounts, so it is at best R-unmatched-budget; no R-strict comparison exists.

comparison: Sec 4.3 (RQ2) Table 4: Baseline Prompt vs Optimized ZeroFalse Prompt, per model
model_config: Same model within each pair (10 LLMs), temperature 0, schema-constrained JSON output
dataset_metric: OWASP Java Benchmark and OpenVuln (58 real-world alerts); F1
budget_control: Not controlled; the optimized prompt is defined as "augmenting the baseline" with trace, rubric and checklist (longer). On OpenVuln the paper reports fewer context-overflow failures for mixtral with the optimized prompt (14 -> 7), so the OpenVuln code context is not a strict superset, but no token counts per arm are given
arm_a: Optimized: rule ID, alert message, code + "complete annotated source-to-sink trace, a CWE-specific micro-rubric encoding domain knowledge, and a structured adjudication checklist"
arm_b: Baseline: "the rule ID, the alert message, and a local code snippet surrounding the dataflow steps" (5 lines around each step on OpenVuln; whole test file on OWASP)
other_changes: No pipeline component, but the optimized arm bundles non-representation content (CWE domain-knowledge rubric and an adjudication checklist, i.e. a prompt-paradigm change) with the dataflow trace
delta: Table 4 OpenVuln F1 improvement per model from -0.243 (gemini-2.5-pro) to +0.381 (gpt-oss-20b), e.g. gpt-5 0.621 -> 0.955 (+0.334); OWASP from -0.104 (deepseek-r1) to +0.194. The +0.176 OpenVuln average is the mean of the ten Table 4 values, not stated in the paper (absolute F1 units)
rationale: Same model and decoding per pair, and only prompt content differs, but the structured arm is the baseline augmented with trace + rubric + checklist and no budget is controlled. The gain therefore mixes representation, domain knowledge and instruction scaffolding with added context.

comparison: Sec 5.4 (Q3) Table 4: MulVul (Full) vs w/o Retrieval
model_config: GPT-4o as the Router/Detector execution model in both arms (Claude Opus 4.5 as the prompt-evolution model); whether prompts were re-evolved without retrieval is not reported
arm_a: Code + agent-invoked retrieval of SCALE-structured labeled examples from a knowledge base (global retrieval for the Router, contrastive in-category/hard-negative retrieval for Detectors)
arm_b: Same agents and evolved prompts without the retrieval tools
other_changes: Removes the retrieval stage (UniXcoder + FAISS knowledge base of labeled training examples) and the agents' retrieval tool calls; the prompt-evolution fitness was computed "with retrieved evidence"
rationale: The ablation removes a module, "Removing evidence retrieval causes the largest performance drop", where the retrieved content is labeled vulnerability examples from a knowledge base, not an alternative representation of the input code. It is a same-model retrieval-component ablation.

comparison: Sec 4 cross-representation probe, Table 5 (and Table 4/6): Text Pilot Qwen3-8B weights on raw text vs pruned AST input
model_config: Identical: the same Text Pilot LoRA checkpoint (Qwen3-8B), "Same model weights applied to two input formats"; unified system prompt with only a "minimal representation-specific preamble" differing
dataset_metric: OWASP Benchmark v1.2 (N=2,740, 1,325 negatives); FPR, F1, recall, precision
budget_control: Not controlled; the AST arm is longer: AST training runs use 4096 vs 2048 max length "because S-expression linearisation approximately doubles sequence length relative to raw text", and the paper describes AST as "a longer, more deeply nested representation"; inference length limit not reported
arm_a: Pruned Semgrep Generic AST (S-expression) of each Java sample
arm_b: Raw Java source text of the same sample
other_changes: none (no retraining; one-line format preamble differs). The AST input is out-of-distribution for the text-trained adapter
rationale: Model, weights, prompt and dataset are held fixed and only the input encoding changes, but the AST encoding is roughly twice as long with no length control. The authors also show the effect is not a benefit of AST itself ("zero-shot model given the same AST input achieves FPR 0.999"); they frame it as a representation-by-training interaction, so the record's "pure representation-only manipulation" overstates it.

comparison: Sec IV-E (RQ3) Table IV (v1; Table 4 in v2): full Antaeus vs -Local vs -Repo
model_config: Same backbone within each comparison (Claude Opus 4.7, and separately GPT-5.4); same structured-reasoning prompt format
dataset_metric: v1: 28 CVEs from ReposVul (CWE-200, CWE-284); v2: 35 CVEs; number of CVEs detected (true positives)
budget_control: Not controlled; removing either context source shortens the prompt (v2 cost section: "both the function-level grounding and the repository-level bundle dominate its prompt size")
arm_a: Function + local augmentation bundle (depth-one callee signatures/bodies, macros, constants, typedefs) + repository-level context bundle
arm_b: -Local: function + repository bundle only; -Repo: function + local augmentation only
other_changes: -Local: none beyond prompt content. -Repo: also removes an upstream pipeline stage, the bundle is "produced by a repository-level LLM agent" run once per repository
delta: v1 Table IV: Opus 4.7 15 -> 9 (-Local) and 9 (-Repo); GPT-5.4 12 -> 8 and 7 detections (of 28). v2 Table 4: Opus 20 -> 13 and 11; GPT-5.4 14 -> 9 and 8 (of 35)
rationale: Same backbone and data, and -Local only withholds the depth-one program context from the prompt, but the full arm is substantially longer with no budget control, so the comparison measures added context rather than representation alone. The -Repo arm additionally removes an LLM-agent summarization stage and is closer to a component ablation. The record's numbers match v1; v2 enlarges the set to 35 CVEs with different counts.
